name: What should I budget per unit for a small multifamily building in Los Angeles County?

mainEntity.name: How much does it really cost per unit to build a 4- to 20-unit multifamily project in Los Angeles, Glendale, Pasadena, Burbank, or North Hollywood?
mainEntity.text: How much does it really cost per unit to build a 4- to 20-unit multifamily project in Los Angeles, Glendale, Pasadena, Burbank, or North Hollywood?

acceptedAnswer.text: Per-unit cost is one of the most searched but least clearly answered questions because the right number depends on more than size. For small multifamily projects in Los Angeles County, the total budget is shaped by land conditions, demolition, underground parking, utility capacity, finish level, and entitlement complexity. Two projects with the same unit count can differ dramatically in cost if one needs major grading, structural retaining walls, or service upgrades. A useful budgeting approach is to break the project into land-related costs, hard construction costs, soft costs, financing, and contingency. Soft costs often surprise owners because they include design, engineering, surveys, consultants, permit fees, and plan check revisions. In higher-density areas, parking strategy and structural design can move the budget far more than cosmetic selections. Owners should ask for a schematic estimate, a permit-stage estimate, and a GMP or detailed construction estimate before committing. If a contractor only gives a rough cost per square foot without asking about zoning, access, utilities, and parking, the number is not reliable. The safest planning move is to carry a contingency large enough to absorb entitlement changes, utility delays, and scope revisions.
acceptedAnswer.description: Per-unit costs for small multifamily projects in Los Angeles County vary widely based on unit count, parking, soft costs, site conditions, and finish level. In dense submarkets, the biggest cost drivers are excavation, structural system, utility upgrades, fire/life-safety requirements, and entitlement delay. A realistic budget should be built from both hard costs and a separate contingency, not a single square-foot number.
